item.title: Let’s Not Scroll to the Next Forever
item.description:
Social Media

Let’s Not Scroll to the Next Forever

How former CNN correspondent Chris Moody managed to switch off his home internet.

Posted November 17, 2026

Key points
  • Willpower can't compete with billion-dollar algorithms designed to capture our attention.
  • Create phone-free spaces where technology simply doesn't belong.
  • Build systems that make unwanted habits harder, rather than relying on discipline.
  • Choose activities with a clear beginning and end, not endless scrolling.

Chris Moody was a senior political correspondent with CNN for many years and is now a journalism professor at Appalachian State University in Boone, NC. He lives in a log cabin in a mountain hollow with his wife and their three-year-old son. The cabin has no cell signal. Over three years ago, they cancelled their home internet and went with a landline (intended to be a temporary measure for one summer). They write about it all in their Substack, The Opt Outers. I interviewed him about why willpower can’t compete with our devices, and what people who can’t move to the mountains can do instead.

Yael Hallak: I deleted my social media accounts six months ago. Then I came across the password to an old Instagram account, and I'm back to scrolling. I can't move to the mountains. What can we do as a species?

Chris Moody: The tech companies know what grabs our attention, and they feed it to us (that's how they make their money). Billions of dollars are being thrown at us, and no human will ever be able to win that battle every time, whether you're trying to find an old password or simply want to switch your mind off.

So create what I call a Sabbath space — a room, a floor, a corner of the house, where these technologies simply can't go in. Some people go down the route of "landlining," where the phone is left plugged in on the kitchen counter, and you're only allowed to use it there, standing. What would have been three hours on the couch comes down to three minutes. Think about whether you actually need Wi-Fi at all or whether a wired connection in one room would be sufficient. And make the rules when you're sober; you don't want to be relying on yourself when you're drunk.

YK: Why not just go with discipline?

CM: Even if you're not using it, the phone is still calling; it's like the sirens calling out to Odysseus. Every moment is a decision, and decision fatigue wins. That's why we have a scoop of ice cream at 9 p.m. and not at 9 a.m.

I drove fifteen minutes to a studio for this interview. My couch would have been far easier, but it's worth it. When I'm finished in town, the laptop goes down, and at home I couldn't have checked email if I'd wanted to. The people who need me have my landline. I'm not living in the 1890s, more in the 1990s.

YK: During the recent bank and flight outages, I was constantly refreshing X. Information is what makes me feel in control. My husband is always telling me to put the phone down and look out of the window.

CM: Today's channels don't give you any data that's going to help. They just feed an appetite that can't be quenched; they're just empty calories. You can learn what you need from the Sunday New York Times once a week. A reporter on a presidential campaign needs real time. Most people don't.

Look at the boomers, the richest generation in history, spending their days being angry online. Do they have more information? Possibly. Are they any happier? No.

YK: You teach undergrads; how are they getting on?

CM: They know the monster is coming for them and they think they've been had. Some of them, the ones brought up by phone-obsessed parents, are completely radicalised: "I'll never ignore my child the way my own did." When they see my Nokia flip phone, they go absolutely mental, and a few of them come back with "I've got one!" They're just as hooked as everyone else, just as keen to get their hands on one, but they're thinking about it very carefully. I'm hopeful.

YK: So many people want this life. What enabled you to get it?

CM: My first real job post-college was in social media (at the very beginning of it), and I saw what the algorithms did to my friends. I'm an extrovert, a golden retriever when the doorbell rings, and suddenly everyone just went off and into their screens. Mostly it's my wife, really. She's the one who drives it. Left to my own devices, I go with the flow.

YK: What do you do at dinners where everyone's on their phone?

CM: At our place, it just works itself out as we don't have phones. People come and ask for the Wi-Fi password, and I say we don't have one; there's a landline if you want it. They never do. We don't have to take the rubbish we've been given; we can just eat the better stuff.

YK: Is there anything you're missing? Podcasts, audiobooks?

CM: Not at all. I download the episodes in town and listen to them at home whilst doing the dishes. On Friday nights we watch a library DVD on a projector and a pull-down screen. It takes ten minutes to set it up, and that friction is important. Everything has a beginning and an end. It's not "let's just scroll to the next forever." It's: that's all we've got.

YK: So you just have more willpower than the rest of us?

CM: No! I have absolutely no willpower. I'm a disaster. When I'm on the road, and there's Wi-Fi all over the place, I just go absolutely mad and end up with no idea how the time has gotten away from me. The solution is systems, really. Less friction for the good things, more for the bad. In New York, we put our phones in baskets by the door, and we had the router on a timer, which would turn it off from 8 p.m. to 8 a.m. If we're going to rely on willpower, we're all going to fail. We all are.

item.title: A Renewed Humanism
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

A Renewed Humanism

Pope Leo, human dignity, and creativity in the age of AI.

Posted November 17, 2026

Key points
  • Pope Leo's encyclical on human dignity and AI has been praised for its moral seriousness and insight.
  • In part, it helps us to think about the ambiguous nature of language and how that shapes our relation to AI.
  • Today we seem to want clear, straightforward ways of communicating.
  • But perhaps more poetic or artistic modes of speech reveal more about the human condition.
Source: Christian Harb/Unsplash

Pope Leo’s Magnifica Humanitas (2026), subtitled “On Safeguarding the Human Person in the Time of Artificial Intelligence,” has been heralded as one of the most significant and morally serious visions for how humanity ought to think about and navigate the advent of the AI era. Acknowledging “the ambiguity of tools,” which are neither morally good nor bad in and of themselves but “can cause harm when not oriented toward the good,” the Pope insists that the end toward which our aspirations aim is as important as the aspirations themselves.

For Leo, protecting and fostering the dignity of the human person must be the goal of everything we do. Contrasting two images taken from Scripture, the Pope calls us to consider how the desire that orients our ambitions changes the things we create.

In Leo’s first example, the construction of the Tower of Babel (Genesis 11:1–9) is motivated by fear and vainglory:

Fearing being scattered across the earth, they [the builders] sought to guarantee stability and power for themselves, and above all to ‘make a name’ for themselves.” Such motives cannot but end in ruin. Leo continues, “When a city is built on pride and the claim to self-sufficiency, communication breaks down, languages are confused and people no longer understand each other. The result is not unity, but dispersion. Babel thus reveals the limits of any effort that, however grandiose, arises from self-affirmation, sacrifices human dignity for efficiency and aspires to reach heaven without God’s blessing.

Source: Igor Omilaev/Unsplash

In his second, which comes from the Book of Nehemiah, Nehemiah returns to the city of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile only to find it in ruins. Heartbroken, he takes in the destruction in silence. Then, before setting to work, he “convened the families, assigned each of them a section of the wall to rebuild, listened to their concerns, coordinated their efforts and addressed any opposition.”

Nehemiah, that is, kept the dignity of those around him at the center of his project rather than running headlong toward apparent solutions. In so doing, he was able to resurrect what had been lost while simultaneously creating something new. The Pope writes:

The narrative shows how the city is reborn, not through the initiative of one man, but through the shared responsibility of all: men, women, priests, artisans, heads of households and young people all play a part. It is an undertaking with God at the center, which rebuilds relationships before rebuilding with stones. Thus, ancient Jerusalem rediscovers a common language—not one of uniformity, but one of communion, namely the harmony that arises when all persons assume their own role and recognize that their strength comes from the Lord.

What makes these images apt for our current moment—and what many commentators have overlooked—is the role language plays in each. For, if the desire of those constructing the Tower of Babel was to create a single, unified language with which all could understand and be understood, so too is the aim of Artificial Intelligence to provide a kind of totalizing language capable of flattening ambiguity and rendering difference obsolete. And if Nehemiah’s success was rooted in the fact that he sought out the input of those he hoped to serve, and even (perhaps especially) those with whom he disagreed, so too must dialogue be at the foundation of technological advance.

Source: Growtika/Unsplash

Consider another example, this one taken from contemporary fiction, that draws out this tension inherent in language—the tension between the desire to communicate directly, if only superficially, and the desire to express how fraught and complex human experience actually is, even if that expression can only be accomplished indirectly and ambiguously.

It comes from Paul Auster’s great work of metareal fiction City of Glass (1987), in which the story’s chief antagonist Peter Stillman—is he still a man, still human, or has he been deformed by his mad pursuit of “perfectibility”?—obsesses over the duplicity of language, the way one word can mean two equal and opposite things. For instance, the word cleave “means both ‘to join together’ and ‘to break apart.’”

For Stillman, the Genesis narrative to which the Pope alluded “records not only the fall of man, but the fall of language” from clarity to opacity. Once, he conjectures, language was simple, direct, and stated exactly what it meant to say without confusion or ambiguity. There was a time when “words had not been merely appended to things . . . they revealed their essences . . . A thing and its name were interchangeable.” But after the destruction of the Tower of Babel, this was no longer true. Now words conceal as much as they reveal, and deception is built into the very nature of how we communicate.

Driven mad by the desire to use language to reunify what appears to him to be a fractured and fragmentary existence, Stillman sets out to realize a utopian future in which his model of a single, unified language makes absolute knowledge and mastery possible. (Sound familiar?)

If the fall of man also entailed a fall of language, was it not logical to assume that it would be possible to undo the fall, to reverse its effects by undoing the fall of language? . . . If man could learn to speak this original language of innocence, did it not follow that he would thereby recover a state of innocence within himself?

The trouble is that Stillman is not able to conjure up this mythical language model, and his attempts to do so inflict immense suffering on those around him.

Source: Olga Tutunaru/Unsplash

In an ironic twist, Stillman ultimately resorts to deception himself in a vain attempt to accomplish his goal. Creating a character named Henry Dark, a fictional disciple of John Milton, he attributes his most controversial ideas to Dark and even falsifies the historical record to make it appear as though Dark had heralded his, Stillman’s, project over 300 years in advance.

What could offer a better image of the LLMs that seem so powerful and omniscient today—with their false citations and hallucinated facts—than a fictional character invented by a mad genius to dupe others into believing that his language model could solve the mysteries and riddles of the human condition? And yet, what could offer a better reason to hope? For, although Dark was invented by Stillman to serve darker ends, still his creation was—as Pope Leo recently called the craft of writing fiction—a profound “act of humanity,” one which points to the supreme dignity of its author even if he, like many of us today, is too consumed with his utopian ideas to appreciate it.

item.title: Dreaming of Cats and Dogs
item.description:
Dreaming

Dreaming of Cats and Dogs

Tracking the dream interactions of cats, dogs, and humans.

Posted November 17, 2026

Key points
  • Cats and dogs appear in dreams more often than any other animals.
  • Their symbolic meanings include natural wisdom and primal instinct.
  • Growing evidence suggests cats and dogs have dream lives of their own.
Source: Kelly Bulkeley

The deep relationships people form with domestic cats and dogs can be among the strongest emotional bonds in their lives. Since we know that dreams offer an accurate reflection of our most important relationships in waking life, it can be predicted that cats and dogs will appear with some frequency in people’s dreams, and this turns out to be true. Interpreting the symbolic themes and images in these dreams can lead to a variety of psychological insights. They can also lead to a new perspective on the possibility, even the likelihood, that our cats and dogs are dreaming about us.

Who Dreams of Cats and Dogs?

Dream researchers have found that dreaming about animals in general is more frequent for children than for adults, more for tribal communities than for modern Westerners, and more for pregnant women than non-pregnant women. Cats and dogs are usually at the top of the list of most-dreamed about animals, so the distribution patterns found in these studies give us a rough clue about who is most likely to experience feline- and canine-related dreaming.

Who appears in dreams more often, cats or dogs? A review of the collections in the Sleep and Dream Database (SDDb) finds that people dream slightly more about dogs than cats. A search for dream reports of 10+ words in length with at least one reference to a dog-related word found 1,088 instances out of 34,475 dream reports, or 3.2% of the total. A parallel search for dream reports of 10+ words in length with at least one reference to a cat-related word found 759 instances out of 34,475 dream reports, or 2.2% of the total.

Looking at the Hall and Van de Castle norm dreams from the 1950’s, a slight variation appears in relation to gender. The 491 dream reports from the males included 11 (2.2%) with a dog-related word but only 2 (0.4%) with a cat-related word, whereas the 490 dream reports from the females had 10 (2%) with a dog-related word and 9 (1.8%) with a cat-related word.

What Do Dreams of Cats and Dogs Mean?

As with any aspect of dream content, the dreamer’s personal context matters. Here, the relevant factors include whether the dreamer has pets now, grew up with pets, feels anxiety around animals, or considers themselves a “dog person” or a “cat person. It also matters how the dogs or cats appear in the dream: healthy or sick, friendly or aggressive, inside or outside, alive or passed away.

Since ancient times, animals in dreams have been regarded as special bearers of natural wisdom. Modern psychoanalysts regard animals in dreams as symbols of our primal desires and wild instincts. Animals can also appear in dreams as cultural metaphors (e.g., a cat = night hunter, a dog = loyal companion).

An early historical example comes from the medieval Japanese monk and Buddhist teacher Myoe Shonin, who recorded the following in his dream journal in 1206:

“I dreamed of two puppies. One was white and the other was of several, rich colors. The mixed-color dog was attractive beyond limit. Thus I fixed a container full of rice. It seemed to me that all the people there used small, open containers as feeding dishes. (Although the white dog went into a fire, it did not burn.)” (168-169)

Myoe did not interpret his dreams, but rather meditated on their visionary qualities. Here, the dream puppies elicit a vivid experience of amazing beauty, compassion for others, and magical resilience.

An aggressive cat figures as a vivid symbol of danger in a dream reported by Anna Bonus Kingsford in 1877. Kingsford was a medical doctor, animal rights activist, and theosophical mystic whose dream journal included this entry:

"I dreamt that I had a beautiful bird in a cage, and that the cage was placed on a table in a room where there was a cat. I took the bird out of the cage and put him on the table. Instantly the cat sprang upon him and seized him in her mouth. I threw myself upon her and strove to wrest away her prey, loading her with reproaches and bewailing the fate of my beautiful bird. Then suddenly some one said to me, 'You have only yourself to blame for this misfortune. While the bird remained in his cage he was safe. Why should you have taken him out before the eyes of the cat?'” (38)

Kingsford said the dream came at a time when she was on the verge of sharing publicly some of her unusual psycho-spiritual experiences, and she interpreted the dream as an unambiguous warning not to do so.

In his 2003 study of a long dream series from a middle-aged woman (“Barb Sanders”), G. William Domhoff found several reports in which kittens were neglected, deformed, or starving. Sanders’ own cats were healthy and fine, so the dreams seemed to point to an indirect symbolic meaning. A closer look suggested a connection between “stray cats” and “lost men,” who were indeed a major concern and problem in her waking life. (128)

Cats and Dogs as Dreamers

Anyone who has lived with a cat or dog has noticed how at certain points during their sleep they whimper and growl, their muscles and whiskers twitch, and their eyes flutter under their eyelids. If we observed the same behavior in a sleeping human, we would surely assume the person is dreaming. And if we knew that person was fed, cuddled, groomed, and loved by a particular individual, we would be on solid research grounds in predicting that person dreams frequently about the caregiving individual.

How much of this, from the REM-dreaming connection to the interpersonal continuities, applies beyond humans to other animal species? The honest answer is, we do not know. But the tide of scientific evidence is moving towards ever greater recognition in non-human animals of emotion, cognition, and high-order consciousness. Can dreaming be far behind?
